answer: The premise is incorrect. node2vec does not use a pure DFS traversal, and its learned representations are not restricted to DFS-style equivalence. It generates second-order biased random walks controlled by two parameters, the return parameter p and the in-out parameter q. Small q lets walks move outward, which is DFS-like and captures homophily (communities). Large q keeps walks local, which is BFS-like and captures structural equivalence (roles). Because p and q are tunable, the walks interpolate between the two regimes rather than committing to one. The resulting embeddings are fed to skip-gram (word2vec-style) training, so they can reflect both kinds of similarity depending on the chosen parameters.
